records.name: Trabzon
records.current_summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. The absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local safety: the nationwide framework applies here in full.

As documented nationally: an October 2025 draft judicial package would criminalise conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality (up to three years) and same-sex ceremonies (up to four), push gender-affirming care beyond age 25 behind infertility assessments, and expose patients and providers to prosecution — protested by civic groups and the medical association. The national LGBTI monitor's 2025 report describes hostility as explicit state policy: public-institution 'family' directives, a first organisational closure in years, 3 hate-motivated killings, 89 ill-treatment violations and 299 detention decisions. And in July 2025 police mounted mass identity-check roundups in which trans women were detained and their names and images recorded without any stated legal basis — 'profiling', the detainees called it.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW, 29 Oct 2025, reports a leaked omnibus reform draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the Turkish penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four; it would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, mandate permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both healthcare professionals performing such care and patients to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW calls for its withdrawal.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's Human Rights Report 2025, titled "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy, with instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (a striking increase over the prior year), 313 right-to-liberty violations - about 2.5 times the previous year - with 299 detention decisions, freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540, and 40 right-to-association violations including the first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years.

records.name: Uşak
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): interior Aegean; conservative. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey. No province-specific trans-related source exists for this province: the national dossier finds blanket-ban practice nationwide, so the absence of a documented provincial ban is not evidence of permissiveness.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW news release, Oct 29, 2025, reports the leaked omnibus draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" (up to three years in prison) and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with possible pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's 2025 review ("The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People") finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy — "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, with expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings (trans people the most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), 313 liberty violations — about two and a half times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans.

records.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
records.current_summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law for travesti, trans and transgender people alongside the national femicide/travesticide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. Against that: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women in the Constitución neighbourhood, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident. Nationally the climate has turned: 2025 set a record of at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity (+62% on 2024, one every 38 hours, the highest since monitoring began ten years ago), 32% of them inside police stations and penal facilities, with security-force violence multiplying from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), trans women and travestis the majority of victims (142, 62.5%); federal closures of the equality ministry and the national anti-discrimination institute and dismissals of trans public-sector quota hires further erode recourse.
records.current_localsOnly: Gender-marker rectification, the national employment quota for travesti/trans people (administered centrally from this city) and detention placement are resident-facing processes; visitors do not interact with them.

sources.claim: National-scope report (Washington Blade, Apr 10, 2025) on the national framework this city sits under: the administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law (which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs), and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Blade that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

National hate-crime observatory data for 2025 (Agencia Presentes, 19 Mar 2026) — the national monitoring record this city sits under: at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record at one crime every 38 hours. 32% of crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases); most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

National-framework source: via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty — inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere — prohibiting those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

records.name: Santa Catarina
records.current_summary: Direction: worse than national — the only Brazilian state to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and the venue of a nationally decisive refusal. Lei 19.686 of 21 January 2026 requires every educational institution in the state — basic, fundamental, secondary, technical and higher — to provide bathrooms separately by sex, banning shared or unisex installation and use, with fines of up to R$10,000; a second bill approved 22 December 2025 extends the ban to state and municipal public administration bodies; a third, tabled October 2025, would restrict school and locker-room use to the sex recorded on the birth certificate — continued legislative escalation rather than a one-off. The nationally decisive case arose here: a trans woman was refused entry to the women's bathroom by staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre, urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to take public transport home; on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules. In the other direction, Florianópolis has a visible LGBTQ tourism scene with pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages and marker changes; nationwide legal rights are identical, so visitors see the same federal protections as elsewhere. Caveat: state violence statistics sit atop the country's nationally leading lethality and should be read partly as reporting density rather than as gender-specific exposure.
records.current_localsOnly: School-bathroom rules, birth-certificate marker procedures and employment provisions are resident-facing; a visitor never enrols or works here.
records.current_outOfScope: General violent-crime exposure in this state mirrors the country's nationally leading lethality and is a risk to any resident or visitor regardless of gender identity; it does not move trans-specific risk.

sources.claim: Encyclopaedic national-rights page containing Santa Catarina-specific entries: the state's constitution (anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002) lists sexual orientation among non-discrimination grounds but, as of 2019, does not address discrimination against transgender people; from 2020 people in Santa Catarina obtain documents recording non-binary gender judicially or through notarial offices even though no specific law prescribes it; in Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. National framework claimed by the record: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013 (CNJ Resolution 175/2013) and the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling making discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation/gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Outright International country page: constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions following the 2019 Supreme Court ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, yet a deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee (a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019) for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy, and the Superior Court of Justice ruled nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity. National-framework source kept per rule 5: the record claims nationwide legal protections identical for this state's visitors and no region-specific source covers that claim.

Law-firm guide for expats, updated 5 April 2026: names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name/gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories (spousal residence permit), foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes, joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed (STF RE 846.102, 2015), gender-marker changes proceed without surgery, and the STF's ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

records.name: Antioquia
records.current_summary:
Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans killings. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a 32-year-old trans woman, Sara Millerey González Borja, was beaten and thrown into a waterway while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries. She was the third LGBT person killed in Bello that year — the first two were gay men — and the case triggered vigils, protests in several cities and a presidential order to investigate, amid a national tally of 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

The national frame around that series, as documented: more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups in at least one southern department have circulated flyers announcing 'social cleansing' against trans women, in territories where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement. The surviving record supports a lethal concentration around Antioquia's metro area — three municipal killings within four months — and documents no province-level protection machinery specific to it.

sources.claim: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups circulating in Caquetá - where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement - distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there were forced to flee after death threats. Retained per rule 5: this supports the record's national-frame claims (2023-24 kill tallies and the southern-department social-cleansing flyers) and no region-specific Antioquia source covers them.

records.name: Bogota Capital District
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Bogotá Capital District: the best-documented trans community and services in the country, alongside a documented police-violence pattern in its tolerance zone. Regional evidence: Red Comunitaria Trans reported police shouting at, baton-beating and shooting at trans sex workers at 3:50 a.m. on a central street (the district mayor's office took up the case); two trans women were killed within hours of each other on the night of 2 January 2026 (a 24-year-old in Engativá, a 20-year-old in Florida Blanca); a 32-year-old trans activist was found dead in the eastern hills in December 2023, with the press itself framing 'the recurring mechanisms in crimes against trans women'. The district's own law journal published a study of violence against trans people in the Santa Fe tolerance zone, where sector expulsions push people into other localities. Mass identity-check operations: 200+ officers in San Bernardo (April 2025) and over 1,200 uniformed officers with background and migrant control in Santa Fe (January 2026) - a visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá is therefore statistically likely to be in the path of a sweep. Scored relative to the national score (0.52) for Colombia.

sources.claim: El País in English (April 14, 2025): the transphobic murder that shocked the country - Sara Millerey, 32, a trans woman, beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello (Antioquia) on 4 April 2025; national context: 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025, presidential call to investigate, vigils in several cities. Cited in this record as national lethal-violence context.

NOTE: not retrievable at fetch time (the CNN page returned only ad-feedback widgets); the underlying article covers attacks against LGBTQ people in Colombia in the context of the Millerey case (per URL slug, Aug 6 2025).

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Colombia overview is the national framework every visitor to Bogotá Capital District stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016 (making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so); adoption equality came in 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; and transgender people have had a right to change legal gender recognised since 1993, reinforced by a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling allowing civil-registry change without a family court. It also records Bogotá-specific facts: a 2012 ruling let a transgender woman choose her own hairstyle and makeup in prison, Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá, pride parades in Bogotá number among the country's large LGBTQ events, and a Washington Post report describes thriving gay neighbourhoods in Bogotá. Beginning in 2026, nonbinary and transgender options are offered on the national identity card.

sources.title: Diversidad sexual en Colombia - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
sources.claim: Spanish Wikipedia's Colombia overview confirms the national baseline a Bogotá visitor stands under: in November 2015 the Constitutional Court approved adoption by same-sex couples and in April 2016 it approved same-sex marriage; the current documentation framework recognises four identity markers - female (F), male (M), trans (T) and non-binary (NB); and rulings T-033 of 2022 and T-527 of 2024 protected the right to gender identity and its recording. Despite the anti-discrimination laws, the page notes that prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the population - context relevant to a visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá.

records.name: Comunidad de Madrid
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Madrid (Chueca): among the most visible LGBT urban scenes in Europe; total anonymity in daily life; Pride among the continent's largest. Regional evidence: the one community that has used its own legislative power to narrow trans law - Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023 (both 27 December 2023) amended the community's own 2016 gender-identity law and its anti-LGBTBI law on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, stripping the provisions that obliged educational institutions; Ley 1/2022 centres parents as primary responsible parties and structures school opt-outs (the 'pin parental' mechanism in Madrid schools). Evidentiary caveat: Madrid's citizens report LGTBI hate-crime offences to reporting services more than any other community's, so low recorded hostility here is not available as an alibi - the divergence is statutory, not statistical. Scored relative to the national score (0.88) for Spain.
records.current_localsOnly: Resident-facing: the 2023 community-level amendments that removed the 2016 trans-law obligations on educational institutions, and the 2022 education law's parental-primary-responsibility and school opt-out mechanism ("pin parental"), shape school environments for local families.

sources.claim: Official text (BOE) of Ley 4/2023 (28 February 2023), "for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGTBI people": establishes self-ID legal gender recognition (16+, no diagnosis), broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy. National framework that Madrid's 2023 amendments sit beside.

Human Rights Watch (Feb 2023): "Victory in Fight for Gender Recognition in Spain" - hails Spain's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory after years of activism. National framework context.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles three statutes - what Law 4/2023 does and does not do; the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 of the Penal Code (gender identity/expression motives); and the hate offences of Article 510 CP extended to trans/LGBTI people. National framework context.

sources.title: Diversidad sexual en Madrid - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Madrid-specific LGBT page documents Madrid as one of Europe's main LGBT hubs and backs the record's route-3 claims about scene visibility: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2005, Madrid Pride (MADO), held annually in late June/early July, is described as one of the largest Pride events in the world drawing millions of attendees, and the Chueca district is the epicentre of the community. It also records local institutions: COGAM, founded 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation, Madrid's city government runs an Oficina de Atencion a la Diversidad Sexual y de Genero, and Arcopoli focuses on fighting discrimination and violence. Crucially for a traveler assessment, the article states that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in Madrid and that marginalised LGBT groups, such as migrants and trans people, face additional barriers.

sources.title: Ley trans (España) - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
sources.claim: This Spanish Wikipedia page on trans law is the national-framework document the Madrid region record stands under: it records that the Comunidad de Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and Region de Murcia (following Extremadura in 2015), which is the 2016 regional statute that Ley 17/2023 later amended. It also covers the state-level Ley 4/2023 (Organic Law of 28 February 2023) on gender self-determination and the framework with which regional statutes like Madrid's must comply, giving the statutory floor a trans traveler in the region stands under.
